properties.name: Definition: a solution of n! + 1 = m^2
properties.statement: A solution is a pair of positive integers (n, m) with n! + 1 = m^2, where n! = 1 * 2 * ... * n. Equivalently, n is a solution index when n! + 1 is a perfect square. (Solutions are often called Brown numbers; that name is recalled, not checked.)

IF abc holds THEN finitely many solutions (Overholt)
properties.rule_name: modus ponens under an assumption that is never discharged
properties.warrant: Overholt's cited implication says abc (in a weak form) implies finiteness. This step takes abc up as an ASSUMPTION; nothing in this design proves abc, so the conclusion holds only conditionally and stays open unconditionally.

properties.name: Exhaustion over n = 1..807 with certificates
properties.rule_name: proof by exhaustion over a finite range (computer-assisted, every case certified)
properties.warrant: The four kept records together cover n = 1..807 (202 + 202 + 202 + 201 values, ranges 1-202, 203-404, 405-606, 607-807). For each n they test 20 primes q, each proven prime and odd. Every n other than 4, 5, 7 has some q with (n!+1)^((q-1)/2) = -1 mod q, so by the lemma n!+1 is not a square. n = 4, 5, 7 are squares by the known-solutions proposition. The range stops at 807 by the host's digit budget, not by any mathematical reason; nothing here concerns n > 807.

properties.name: Exhibit the three solutions by exact computation
properties.rule_name: proof by construction (exhibiting witnesses), checked by exact computation
properties.warrant: By the definition, (n, m) is a solution when n! + 1 = m^2. The kept calc record computes 4!+1, 5!+1, 7!+1 exactly as 25, 121, 5041, returns their square roots exactly as 5, 11, 71 (not rounded), and checks m*m == n!+1 for each.

properties.name: n! is divisible by every prime up to n
properties.rule_name: direct proof from the definition of n!
properties.warrant: If p <= n then p is one of the factors 1, 2, ..., n, so p divides n! and n! + 1 is 1 mod p; 1 = 1^2 is a nonzero square mod p. Hence every congruence condition modulo such p is satisfied by n! + 1, and cannot exclude it from being a square.

properties.name: Fermat gives the non-residue certificate
properties.rule_name: direct proof by cases (q divides v / q does not divide v), from Fermat's little theorem
properties.warrant: Suppose v = m^2. If q divides v then v^((q-1)/2) is 0 mod q. Otherwise q does not divide m, so v^((q-1)/2) = m^(q-1), which is 1 mod q by Fermat's little theorem (a = m). Since q is odd, q > 2 and 1 is not congruent to -1 mod q. So in neither case is v^((q-1)/2) congruent to -1; contrapositively, a value -1 rules out a square. q and v are arbitrary: nothing beneath fixes them.

properties.objective: State honestly what is known about n! + 1 = m^2: what is proven, what is computed and only for which n, what is conditional on an unproven conjecture, and what is open

properties.answer: Keep abc as an open, undischarged assumption, so 'finitely many solutions' stays conditional; Mochizuki's claimed proof stays contested with the Scholze–Stix objection standing.
properties.context_setter: Finiteness of the solutions is reached here only by assuming the abc conjecture. Mochizuki claims a proof of abc; Scholze and Stix object to it.

I have not adjudicated the dispute and do not propose to.

properties.name: Claim: the abc conjecture is proven (Mochizuki, IUT) - CONTESTED
properties.source: CITED: Mochizuki posted the papers in 2012; they were published in Publications of the RIMS in 2021 (recalled). Objection: Peter Scholze and Jakob Stix (2018 report) argue that Corollary 3.12 has a gap. The mainstream view, as I recall it, is that abc remains open.
properties.statement: CONTESTED CLAIM, not accepted here: Shinichi Mochizuki's inter-universal Teichmuller theory proves the abc conjecture. If it were accepted, req:conj-finitely-many would follow unconditionally through Overholt's implication. This design does not use it as a premise.

properties.name: The abc conjecture (OPEN; assumed only where stated)
properties.source: CITED: formulated by Joseph Oesterle and David Masser (1985). A claimed proof by Shinichi Mochizuki (inter-universal Teichmuller theory, posted 2012, published 2021 in Publ. RIMS) is not accepted by most number theorists; see req:claim-abc-proved-iut and its objection.
properties.statement: OPEN CONJECTURE (assumption). For every epsilon > 0 there is a constant K(epsilon) such that for all coprime positive integers a, b, c with a + b = c, c < K(epsilon) * rad(abc)^(1 + epsilon), where rad(x) is the product of the distinct primes dividing x. Overholt's argument is recalled as needing only a weaker form; the exact weak form used is not recalled.

properties.name: Brocard's problem: the only solutions are n = 4, 5, 7 (OPEN)
properties.source: CITED: posed by Henri Brocard (1876, and again 1885 - years recalled, not checked) and independently by Srinivasa Ramanujan (1913, as a problem in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society - question number not recalled). Its status as open is my recollection; the observer holds the sources.
properties.statement: OPEN CONJECTURE. The only positive-integer solutions of n! + 1 = m^2 are (n, m) = (4, 5), (5, 11) and (7, 71). Nobody has proven or refuted this.

properties.name: Only finitely many solutions (OPEN unconditionally)
properties.source: Weaker than Brocard's conjecture (req:conj-brocard implies it). Known only conditionally (Overholt 1993, cited at req:thm-overholt-abc-implies-finite).
properties.statement: OPEN unconditionally. The equation n! + 1 = m^2 has only finitely many solutions in positive integers. It is not known to hold without assuming an unproven conjecture; in this design it is reached only on the assumption of the abc conjecture.

properties.name: Lemma: primes up to n can never rule a solution out
properties.source: Elementary; argued in this design from the definition (step inf:no-small-prime-obstruction). The remark about why the problem is hard is my gloss, not a cited result.
properties.statement: For every n and every prime p <= n, n! + 1 is congruent to 1 modulo p, which is a nonzero square modulo p. So no congruence modulo a prime p <= n can show that n! + 1 is not a square; any modular certificate for a given n must use a prime q > n. This is one reason elementary congruence arguments cannot settle the problem for all n at once.

properties.name: Lemma: a Fermat non-residue certificate rules out a square
properties.source: Elementary; argued in this design from Fermat's little theorem (step inf:nonresidue-certificate).
properties.statement: Let q be an odd prime and v an integer. If v^((q-1)/2) is congruent to -1 modulo q, then v is not a perfect square. (If v = m^2: when q divides v, v^((q-1)/2) is 0 mod q, not -1; otherwise q does not divide m and v^((q-1)/2) = m^(q-1) is 1 mod q by Fermat's little theorem, and 1 is not -1 mod q because q > 2.)

properties.name: Objection: Scholze-Stix gap in IUT Corollary 3.12
properties.source: CITED: Peter Scholze and Jakob Stix, 'Why abc is still a conjecture' (2018 report, recalled from memory). Mochizuki disputes the objection. Not adjudicated here.
properties.statement: OBJECTION to req:claim-abc-proved-iut: the argument for Corollary 3.12 of inter-universal Teichmuller theory III is said to contain a gap, so the claimed proof of abc is not established.

properties.name: Bounded result: for n <= 807 the only solutions are n = 4, 5, 7
properties.source: Computed in this design: brocard-search-part1-n1-202, part2-n203-404, part3-n405-606, part4-n607-807 (.calc.json), combined with the lemma.
properties.statement: FOR A BOUNDED RANGE ONLY (computer-certified; the steps await the owner's or a checker's confirmation): for 1 <= n <= 807, n! + 1 is a perfect square exactly when n = 4, 5 or 7. For every other n in that range, one of 20 primes q between 1031 and 1171 (each proven prime by calc) gives (n! + 1)^((q-1)/2) congruent to -1 mod q, a certificate that n! + 1 is not a square (req:lem-nonresidue-certificate). Exactly 3 of the 807 values survive all 20 tests: n = 4, 5, 7, which are squares (req:prop-known-solutions). Says NOTHING about n > 807. Stopped at 807 because 808! has 2,001 digits, past the flo2.io calc host's 2,000-digit budget for an exact number (record brocard-search-ceiling.calc.json, not computed).

properties.name: The three known solutions: (4,5), (5,11), (7,71)
properties.source: Computed in this design with flo2 calc; the values were also given in the literature (Brocard, Ramanujan) but are checked here, not assumed.
properties.statement: (n, m) = (4, 5), (5, 11) and (7, 71) are solutions: 4! + 1 = 25 = 5^2, 5! + 1 = 121 = 11^2, 7! + 1 = 5041 = 71^2. Shown by exact computation (record brocard-known-solutions.calc.json: the square roots come back exact, 5, 11 and 71, and each squared equals n! + 1).

properties.name: Published computer searches: no new solutions far beyond 807 (cited, evidence only)
properties.source: CITED with uncertainty: Bruce C. Berndt and William F. Galway, Ramanujan Journal, 2000 - no new solutions for n up to 10^9 (recalled). Later: Robert Matson (around 2017, up to about 10^12?) and Ethan Epstein and Kevin Glickman (around 2020, up to about 10^15?) - names, bounds and years recalled with low confidence. Earlier small searches (e.g. Gupta, 1935, to n = 63) also recalled with low confidence.
properties.statement: CITED COMPUTATIONAL CLAIM, not reproduced here, evidence only: published searches found no solution other than n = 4, 5, 7 for n up to at least 10^9; later searches are recalled as extending this to about 10^12 and then 10^15. The exact bounds and years beyond the first are uncertain. Like the search in this design, it covers finitely many n and proves nothing about larger n.

properties.name: Unconditional: solutions have density zero (Berend–Osgood 1992, citation checked)
properties.source: CHECKED 2026-10-18 against the literature (search results citing it): D. Berend and C. F. Osgood, "On the equation P(x) = n! and a question of Erdős", J. Number Theory 42 (1992), 189–193 — without assuming abc, for any polynomial P of degree >= 2 the set of n with an integer solution of P(x) = n! has density zero. Paper itself not read.
properties.statement: CITED, unconditional, proven in the literature, not here: the set of n for which n! + 1 is a perfect square has natural density zero. This is the special case P(x) = x^2 - 1 of a result on P(x) = n! for polynomials P of degree at least 2. It does NOT give finiteness: a density-zero set can still be infinite.

properties.name: Fermat's little theorem (cited)
properties.source: CITED, not proven in this design: stated by Pierre de Fermat (1640, in a letter); a proof was published by Euler (1736 is my recollection of the year). Standard in any elementary number theory text. Recalled from memory; the owner is asked whether to take it as given.
properties.statement: For every prime q and every integer a not divisible by q, a^(q-1) is congruent to 1 modulo q.

properties.name: Overholt: abc implies finitely many solutions (cited implication)
properties.source: CHECKED 2026-10-18 against the literature (search results citing it): M. Overholt, "The diophantine equation n! + 1 = m^2", Bull. London Math. Soc. 25 (1993), p. 104 — a WEAK form of the abc conjecture implies finitely many solutions. Paper itself not read.
properties.statement: CITED IMPLICATION, proven in the literature, not here: if the abc conjecture holds (Overholt is recalled as needing only a weak form of it), then n! + 1 = m^2 has only finitely many solutions. It gives no explicit bound on n, so even granting abc it does not settle Brocard's conjecture.
